{{Short description|Sphere-like surface}}
{{about|the geometrical figure or shape|the species of mushrooms|Psilocybe ovoideocystidiata}}
[[File:Ovoid-definition.svg|thumb|To the definition of an ovoid: t tangent, s secant line]]
In projective geometry an '''ovoid''' is a sphere like pointset (surface) in a projective space of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}}. Simple examples in a [[real projective space]] are hyperspheres ([[quadric]]s). The essential geometric properties of an ovoid <math>\mathcal O</math> are:
#  Any line intersects <math>\mathcal O</math> in at most 2 points, 
# The tangents at a point cover a [[hyperplane]] (and nothing more), and 
# <math>\mathcal O</math> contains no lines. 
Property 2) excludes degenerated cases (cones,...). Property 3) excludes ruled surfaces (hyperboloids of one sheet, ...).

An ovoid is the spatial analog of an [[Oval (projective plane)|oval]] in a projective plane.

An ovoid is a special type of a ''[[quadratic set]].''

Ovoids play an essential role in constructing examples of [[Möbius plane]]s and higher dimensional Möbius geometries.

== Definition of an ovoid ==
* In a projective space of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}} a set <math>\mathcal O</math> of points is called an '''ovoid''', if
: (1) Any line {{mvar|g}} meets <math>\mathcal O</math> in at most 2 points.
In the case of <math>|g\cap\mathcal O|=0</math>, the line is called a ''passing'' (or ''exterior'') ''line'', if <math>|g\cap\mathcal O|=1</math> the line is a ''tangent line'', and if <math>|g\cap\mathcal O|=2</math> the line is a ''secant line''.
: (2) At any point <math>P \in \mathcal O</math> the tangent lines through {{mvar|P}} cover a hyperplane, the ''tangent hyperplane'', (i.e., a projective subspace of dimension {{math|''d'' − 1}}).
: (3) <math>\mathcal O</math> contains no lines.

From the viewpoint of the hyperplane sections, an ovoid is a rather homogeneous object, because
*For an ovoid <math>\mathcal O</math> and a hyperplane <math>\varepsilon</math>, which contains at least two points of <math>\mathcal O</math>, the subset <math>\varepsilon \cap \mathcal O</math> is an ovoid (or an oval, if {{math|1=''d'' = 3}}) within the hyperplane <math>\varepsilon</math>.

For ''finite'' projective spaces of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}} (i.e., the point set is finite, the space is pappian<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=28}}</ref>), the following result is true:
* If <math>\mathcal O</math> is an ovoid in a ''finite'' projective space of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}}, then {{math|1=''d'' = 3}}.
:(In the finite case, ovoids exist only in 3-dimensional spaces.)<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=48}}</ref>
*In a finite projective space of order {{math|''n'' >2}} (i.e. any line contains exactly {{math|''n'' + 1}} points) and dimension {{math|1=''d'' = 3}} any pointset <math>\mathcal O</math> is an ovoid [[if and only if]] <math>|\mathcal O|=n^2+1</math> and no three points are [[collinear]] (on a common line).<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=48}}</ref>

Replacing the word ''projective'' in the definition of an ovoid by ''affine'', gives the definition of an ''affine ovoid''.

If for an (projective) ovoid there is a suitable hyperplane <math>\varepsilon</math> not intersecting it, one can call this hyperplane the ''hyperplane <math>\varepsilon_\infty</math> at infinity'' and the ovoid becomes an affine ovoid in the [[affine space]] corresponding to <math>\varepsilon_\infty</math>. Also, any affine ovoid can be considered a projective ovoid in the projective closure (adding a hyperplane at infinity) of the affine space.

== Examples ==

=== In real projective space (inhomogeneous representation) ===
#<math>\mathcal O=\{(x_1,...,x_d)\in {\mathbb R}^d \; |\; x_1^2+\cdots +x_d^2=1\}\ ,</math> (hypersphere)
#<math>\mathcal O=\{(x_1,...,x_d)\in {\mathbb R}^d \; | x_d=x_1^2+\cdots +x_{d-1}^2\; \} \; \cup \; \{\text{point at infinity of } x_d\text{-axis}\}</math>

These two examples are ''quadrics'' and are projectively equivalent.

Simple examples, which are not quadrics can be obtained by the following constructions:
: (a) Glue one half of a hypersphere to a suitable hyperellipsoid in a [[smoothness|smooth]] way.
: (b) In the first two examples replace the expression {{math|''x''<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>}} by {{math|''x''<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup>}}.

''Remark:'' The real examples can not be converted into the complex case (projective space over <math>{\mathbb C}</math>). In a complex projective space of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}} there are no ovoidal quadrics, because in that case any non degenerated quadric contains lines.

But the following method guarantees many non quadric ovoids:
* For any ''non-finite'' projective space the existence of ovoids can be proven using ''transfinite induction''.<ref>W. Heise: ''Bericht über <math>\kappa</math>-affine Geometrien'', Journ. of Geometry 1 (1971), S. 197–224, Satz 3.4.</ref><ref>[[Francis Buekenhout|F. Buekenhout]]: ''A Characterization of Semi Quadrics'', Atti dei Convegni Lincei 17 (1976), S. 393-421, chapter 3.5</ref>

=== Finite examples ===
* Any ovoid <math>\mathcal O</math> in a ''finite'' projective space of dimension {{math|1=''d'' = 3}} over a field {{mvar|K}} of [[Characteristic (field)|characteristic]] {{math|≠ 2}} is a ''quadric''.<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=49}}</ref>

The last result can not be extended to even characteristic, because of the following non-quadric examples:
* For <math>K=GF(2^m),\; m </math> odd and <math>\sigma</math> the automorphism <math> x \mapsto x^{(2^{\frac{m+1}{2}})}\; ,</math>
the pointset 
:<math>\mathcal O=\{(x,y,z)\in K^3 \; |\; z=xy+x^2x^\sigma+y^\sigma \} \; \cup \; \{\text{point of infinity of the } z\text{-axis}\}</math> is an ovoid in the 3-dimensional projective space over {{mvar|K}} (represented in inhomogeneous coordinates).
:Only when {{math|1=''m'' = 1}} is the ovoid <math>\mathcal O</math> a quadric.<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|page=52}}</ref>
:<math>\mathcal O</math> is called the '''Tits-Suzuki-ovoid'''.

== Criteria for an ovoid to be a quadric ==
An ovoidal quadric has many symmetries. In particular:
* Let be <math>\mathcal O</math> an ovoid in a projective space <math>\mathfrak P</math> of dimension {{math|''d'' ≥ 3}} and <math>\varepsilon</math> a hyperplane. If the ovoid is symmetric to any point  <math>P \in \varepsilon \setminus \mathcal O</math> (i.e. there is an involutory perspectivity with center <math>P</math> which leaves <math>\mathcal O</math> invariant), then <math>\mathfrak P</math> is pappian and <math>\mathcal O</math> a quadric.<ref>H. Mäurer: ''Ovoide mit Symmetrien an den Punkten einer Hyperebene'', Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 45 (1976), S.237-244</ref>
*An ovoid <math>\mathcal O</math> in a projective space <math>\mathfrak P</math> is a quadric, if the group of projectivities, which leave  <math>\mathcal O</math> invariant operates 3-transitively on <math>\mathcal O</math>, i.e. for two triples <math>A_1,A_2,A_3,\; B_1,B_2,B_3</math> there exists a projectivity <math>\pi</math> with <math>\pi(A_i)=B_i,\; i=1,2,3</math>.<ref>[[Jacques Tits|J. Tits]]: ''Ovoides à Translations'', Rend. Mat. 21 (1962), S. 37–59.</ref>

In the finite case one gets from [[Segre's theorem]]:
* Let be <math>\mathcal O</math> an ovoid in a ''finite'' 3-dimensional desarguesian projective space <math>\mathfrak P</math> of ''odd'' order, then <math>\mathfrak P</math> is pappian and <math>\mathcal O</math> is a quadric.

== Generalization: semi ovoid ==
Removing condition (1) from the definition of an ovoid results in the definition of a '''semi-ovoid''':
:A point set <math>  \mathcal O</math> of a projective space is called a ''semi-ovoid'' if
the following conditions hold:
:(SO1) For any point <math>P \in \mathcal O</math> the tangents through point <math>P</math> exactly cover a hyperplane. 
: (SO2)  <math>\mathcal O</math> contains no lines.

A semi ovoid is a special ''semi-quadratic set''<ref>[[Francis Buekenhout|F. Buekenhout]]: ''A Characterization of Semi Quadrics'', Atti dei Convegni Lincei 17 (1976), S. 393-421.</ref> which is a generalization of a ''[[quadratic set]]''. The essential difference between a semi-quadratic set and a quadratic set is the fact, that there can be lines which have 3 points in common with the set and the lines are not contained in the set.

Examples of semi-ovoids are the sets of isotropic points of an [[hermitian form]]. They are called ''hermitian quadrics''.

As for ovoids in literature there are criteria, which make a semi-ovoid to a hermitian quadric.
See, for example.<ref>K.J. Dienst: ''Kennzeichnung hermitescher Quadriken durch Spiegelungen'', Beiträge zur geometrischen Algebra (1977), Birkhäuser-Verlag, S. 83-85.</ref>

Semi-ovoids are used in the construction of examples of Möbius geometries.
